title: A little winter adventure, right outside our door.
summary: Facebook Marketplace snowshoes, ski poles from a local free group, and a winter memory with James right outside our home.
search: The journal / A winter memory Right outside home · From the family albumA little winter adventure, right outside our door.Facebook Marketplace snowshoes, ski poles from a local free group, and a winter memory with James right outside our home.Published October 22, 2026 · Updated October 25, 2026Secondhand snowshoes, free-group ski poles, and snow on our doorstep. Facebook Marketplace snowshoes, ski poles from our local free group, fresh snow underfoot, and James beside me—we were ready for a spontaneous winter adventure before we even had to leave the front door. ❄️❤️ I love a secondhand find, especially when it gives us a chance to try something together without spending a fortune before we even know whether we’ll enjoy it. We had snow, we had the gear, and we didn’t have to pack the car. A pretty good start! The grin came before the first step. Michael was still bent over the bindings, getting a snowshoe settled around a boot, and James was already beaming. Purple mittens up, knitted hat on, snow collecting on his navy jacket. There is a photograph of him looking straight at me with that enormous smile. I am very glad I kept taking pictures. Getting the bindings ready. The grin was already there. The poles from the free group were propped in the snow nearby. The snowshoes had their next pair of feet in them. I like seeing secondhand things at work like this: someone else has finished with them, and here they are in the middle of our afternoon. Then the little sequence unfolds: a step, a turn toward Michael, a look back at the camera. The blue frames stand out against the white. Snow is falling through every photograph. You can almost lose the houses and trees in it, but there is no missing his face. Purple mittens, blue snowshoes, and that face.Looking back, still smiling. Room to try. Room to finish. With James, planning an activity also means thinking about how to make it understandable and give him ways to tell us what he needs. Picture cards—including familiar cards for families who use PECS—can be part of that preparation: snowshoes, coat, mittens, outside, then home. Something concrete to look at while we talk about what’s coming next. And communication matters throughout the adventure. “Help,” “break,” “finished,” and “more” deserve just as much room as the plan itself. I want us to make space for what James has to say, however he communicates it. Being right outside our home gives us a little breathing room, too. We can take our time getting used to something new, keep the outing short, or head back inside. There’s no admission fee to justify and no long drive home if it turns out to be a five-minute kind of adventure. As a parent and caregiver, I appreciate that. I want James to have opportunities to try things, and I want those opportunities to fit him. Sometimes that takes preparation, visual supports, and the flexibility to let the day unfold differently than I imagined. I love our bigger outings, but I want to remember these days just as clearly: a Facebook Marketplace find, the generosity of a local free group, and time outside with my boy. Looking through the rest of these pictures, I keep coming back to how close everything was: Michael beside James, the poles within reach, the door nearby. We had room to try something without having to commit the whole day to it. And now we have the small details to remember: purple mittens held up in the snow, a parent crouched over a binding, that last look back. I want these in the family album alongside the trips we planned for months. There is a lot of life to enjoy just beyond the front door. ❤️❄️ More from the family album · six photographsA turn toward Michael.One snowshoe up.A few steps into the snow.The view from a few steps behind.Blue frames against all that white.Good company, close to home. title: Thank you for passing it along.
